title: The Christmas Morning Deposition.
subtitle: Under oath, this all happened.
body_html:
“…”

Q.

On Christmas Eve, this very year, I lay quietly in my bed. I did not rustle the sheets, given the court order enjoining me from “sheet rustling.” I breathed slowly—I’ve heard low, slow breaths are calming—and silently. I was listening for a sound – a sound that the fake news media had told me I’d never hear- the ringing bells of Santa’s sleigh.

“There is no Bad Santa,” our President had insisted, but I knew he was wrong.

Late this night, I did hear sounds, though not of ringing bells.

“…”

Hold on, are you recording this? This is a two-party state. You have to tell me when we start recording. We are? Ok. Yes, I consent to this recording.

From outside came the sounds of hissing steam and squeaking metal.

Q.

No, not like Limp Bizkit. Or even Megadeath. Literal metal, not the musical genre of “Metal,” but thank you for checking.

I looked through my window and saw a train standing perfectly still in front of my house.

Q.

Yes, I’m sure it was perfectly still, not just “frozen.” I could tell it was not moving because it was wrapped in an apron of steam. Snowflakes fell lightly around it.

“…”

I know, this is what I’m saying.

“…”

Sorry, this is my testimony. A conductor stood at the open door of one of the cars. He took a look at the large and expensive-looking watch on his wrist,

Q.

Oh, Audemars Piguet. No, they are not on Amazon. The best I have an affiliate link for is the Bulova. Or, look, I wear an Apple Watch. Can I continue?

“…”

Then, I looked up at my window. I put on my slippers and robe. I tiptoed downstairs and out the door.

“…”

I get your point, re: slippers and tiptoeing; however, there is data on this:

there is inadequate evidence to link any particular footwear style with falls. However, it may be possible that it was not the style of footwear, rather how accustomed the individual was to wear that particular style of footwear.1

“…”

“All aboard,” the conductor cried out. I ran up to him.

“Well, he said, “Are you coming?”

“Where?” I asked.

“Why to the [redacted] of course,” was his answer. “This is the [redacted] Express.” I took his outstretched hand, and he pulled me aboard.

The train was filled with other children, all in their pajamas and nightgowns.

Q.

There were no adults other than the conductor that I could see at the time. We sang Christmas carols and ate candies with nougat centers as white as snow.

Q.

I assume it was approved for children with diabetes. There have been advances in nougat science!

We developed a sugar-free nougat recipe by mixing xanthan gum, erythritol, and inulin with egg whites and almonds.2

So you can stop being a grinch?

“…”

We drank hot cocoa as thick and rich as melted chocolate bars.

Q.

This question? I’m actually grateful for it—cacao is a miracle health food. Let me regale you with just some of the health benefits:

Cocoa can lower the leukotriene/ prostacyclin ratio and is shown to have beneficial effects on platelets and possibly inflammation and vessel dilation. They inhibit low-density lipoprotein (LDL) oxidation, raise the high-density lipoprotein (HDL) level and reduce the thrombotic tendency. Their antioxidant catechin content is four times that of tea. They help the body process nitric oxide. Their flavanols and procyanidins have inhibitory effects on hemolysis, they can also attribute as a defense against reactive oxygen species (ROS) and can inhibit their carcinogenic processes. Also they are shown to inhibit growth and polyamine biosynthesis of human colonic cancer cells.3

“…”

Yes, it’s from the journal “Chocolate in Health and Nutrition.” Why do you suspect that it is industry-funded? We have large-scale data, but it’s of low quality. I’ll refer to the review in “Clinical Nutrition,” instead:

Among observational studies, including a total of 1,061,637 participants, the best available evidence suggests that chocolate consumption is associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) death (n = 4 studies), acute myocardial infarction (n = 6), stroke (n = 5) and diabetes (n = 6), although this was based on a weak evidence of credibility. Across meta-analyses of intervention studies, chocolate consumption was positively associated with flow-mediated dilatation at 90–150 min (n = 3) and at 2–18 weeks (n = 3), and insulin resistance markers (n = 2). However, using the GRADE assessment, the evidence for these outcomes was low or very low.4

“…”

Outside, the lights of towns and villages flickered in the distance as the [redacted] Express raced northward.

Soon, there were no more lights to be seen. We traveled through cold, dark forests, where lean wolves roamed,

Q.

I know a fat wolf when I see one! They hadn’t caught the white-tailed rabbits that hid from our train as it (e.g., the [redacted] express) thundered through the quiet wilderness.

We climbed mountains so high it seemed as if we would scrape the moon, like that 3I/ATLAS is about to! But the [redacted] Express never slowed down. Faster and faster we ran along, rolling over peaks and through valleys like a car on a roller coaster.

The mountains turned into hills, the hills to fake-snow-covered plains.

Q.

I mean, I assume it was fake snow. Climate change, you know. We crossed a barren desert of ice—the Great [redacted] Ice Cap. Lights appeared in the distance. They looked like the lights of a strange ocean liner sailing on a frozen sea. “There,” said the conductor, “is the [redacted] Pole.”

“…”

It seems a little pointless to redact which Pole. There are only two.

“…”

Oh, I guess if you include the magnetic poles, there are more. That makes more sense. Shall I continue? The [redacted] Pole. It was a huge city standing alone at the top of the world, filled with factories where every Christmas toy was made. From a supply chain perspective, it seemed strange that it wasn’t in China, but I guess the expertise around toymaking should be diversified.

“…”

Oh, wait—tariffs! It makes more sense now. The [redacted] pole is legally in international waters and thus is under no specific tariff regime. At first, we saw no elves.

Q.

I was worried they had been deported to CECOT. But it turns out, the [redacted] pole is its own Centro de Confinamiento del Navidad. “The elves are gathering up by ICE, except literally Ice, at the center of the city,” the conductor told us. “That is where Santa will give the first gift of Christmas.”

“Who receives the first gift?” we all asked.

“He will choose [redacted].”

“Look,” shouted one of the children, “the elves.” Outside, we saw hundreds of elves, heads down, hooded, being marched into the center of the nightmarish hellscape, but cold. Maybe that was real snow? As our train drew closer to the center of the [redacted] Pole, we slowed to a crawl, so crowded were the streets with Santa’s agents. When the [redacted] Express could go no farther, we stopped, and the conductor led us outside.

We pressed through the crowd to the edge of a large, open circle. In front of us stood Santa’s sleigh. The [redacted] were excited. They pranced and paced, ringing the silver sleigh bells that hung from their [redacted]. It was a magical sound, like nothing I’d ever heard. Across the circle, the elves moved apart, and [redacted] appeared. The [redacted] cheered wildly.

He marched over to us and, pointing to me, said, “Let’s have this fellow here.”

Q.

I was terrified, at first. I mean, look what happened to [redacted]?

He jumped into his sleigh. The conductor handed me up. I sat on Santa’s knee, and he asked, “Now, what would you like for Christmas?”

I knew that I could have any gift I could imagine. But the thing I wanted most for Christmas was not inside Santa’s giant bag. What I wanted more than anything was one ironclad indictment filed by adult prosecutors to bring these people to justice. When I asked, Santa smiled. Then he gave me a hug.

“…”

I know, it’s upsetting that this was his reaction. Eventually, he told [redacted] to cut a bell from a [redacted]’s harness. The [redacted] tossed it up to Santa. He stood, holding the bell high above him, and called out, “The first gift of Christmas!”

Q.

It’s absolutely not what I wanted. I wanted a case filed, a serious case. Not a plea deal, not some *%&$ing bell, handed like that, will distract me. I want justice. All the children want justice. We were abducted. We could not consent to a non-magical train. Why should we be presumed able to consent to a magical train? It’s not like this was high-speed rail in California or some real, actual miracle.

“…”

A clock struck midnight as the elves roared their approval. Santa handed the bell to me, and I put it in my bathrobe pocket. The conductor helped me down from the sleigh. Santa shouted out the reindeer’s names and cracked his whip. His team charged forward and climbed into the air. Santa circled once above us, then disappeared in the cold, dark polar sky.

As soon as we were back inside the [redacted] Express, the other children asked to see the bell. I reached into my pocket, but the only thing I felt was a hole. I had lost the silver bell from Santa Claus’s sleigh. “Let’s hurry outside and look for it,” one of the children said. But the train gave a sudden lurch and started moving. We were on our way home.

It broke my heart to lose the bell.

Q.

Even though I wanted justice, the bell was at least something. When the train reached my house, I sadly left the other children. I stood at my doorway and waved goodbye. The conductor said something from the moving train, but I couldn’t hear him. “What?” I yelled out.

He cupped his hands around his mouth. “[redacted], “he shouted. The [redacted] Express let out a loud blast from its whistle and sped away.

On Christmas morning, my little sister [redacted] and I opened our presents. When it looked as if everything had been unwrapped, Sarah found one last small box behind the tree. It had my name on it. Inside was the silver bell! There was a note: “Found this on the seat of my sleigh. Fix that hole in your pocket.” Signed, “Mr. C.”

I shook the bell. It made no sound.

But my mother said, “Oh, that’s too bad.”

“Yes,” said my father, “it’s broken.”

When I’d shaken the bell, my parents had not heard a sound either. Suspicious, I examined it more closely. Then the bell could be twisted open! Inside, a USB key, wrapped in tinsel!

I stuck the key into my laptop, and, in well-organized folders with clear labeling, were hundreds of thousands of documents, each unredacted and clear.

No wonder Santa was afraid for his life. But maybe, just maybe, justice can now be done.

1

Davis, A., Haines, T., & Williams, C. (2019). Do footwear styles cause falls or increase falls risk in healthy older adults? A systematic review. Footwear Science, 11(1), 13-23.

2

Ottombrino, A., Maurano, F., Montesano, E., Picariello, A., Oiviero, A., & Rossi, M. (2023). Development of functional nougat without diabetic effects in vivo. International Food Research Journal, 30(6), 1401-1407.

3

Castell, M., Pérez-Cano, F. J., & Bisson, J. F. (2012). Clinical benefits of cocoa: An overview. Chocolate in health and nutrition, 265-275.]

4

Nicola Veronese, Jacopo Demurtas, Stefano Celotto, Maria Gabriella Caruso, Stefania Maggi, Francesco Bolzetta, Joseph Firth, Lee Smith, Patricia Schofield, Ai Koyanagi, Lin Yang, Marco Solmi, Brendon Stubbs, Is chocolate consumption associated with health outcomes? An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses, Clinical Nutrition, Volume 38, Issue 3, 2019, Pages 1101-1108, ISSN 0261-5614, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.clnu.2018.05.019.
